questions.q: Zakat is the fourth pillar of Islam.
In Islamic economy, money belongs to Allah and people are merely trustees.
Capitalism focuses on balancing individual and community interests equally.
The concept of wealth includes both goods and services.
Omar Ibn Al-Khattab was the first to establish the state treasury (Beit Al-Mal).
What percentage is typically required for Zakat on wealth?
Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of Islamic Economy?
How many categories of Zakat recipients are mentioned in the Quran?
Which economic system believes that wealth and production means belong to the entire community?
What does "Fay'" refer to in Islamic economics?
Which Caliph fought people who refused to pay Zakat?
What fraction of spoils of war goes to the state according to Islamic law?
Which of the following is a disadvantage of Socialism?
What is the Arabic word from which "Economy" is linguistically derived?
Which is NOT a condition for a commodity in Islamic economics?
What is the definition of Islamic Economy?
questions.m: Islamic Economy refers to the knowledge of practical religious legislations through detailed proofs that regulate earning, spending, and investing money according to Islamic principles and Shariah law. It encompasses the study of how economic activities should be conducted in accordance with Islamic values and teachings.

questions.q: Define "Zakat" and explain its significance in Islam.
questions.m: Zakat is the allocated amount in the wealth of certain individuals for a specific group of people at a certain time. It is the third pillar of Islam and a religious obligation. Zakat is customarily 2.5% (or 1/40) of a Muslim's total disposable wealth after necessities. It serves as a means of purification and is distributed to eight categories of recipients as outlined in the Quran (Surah At-Tawbah 9:60): the poor, the needy, administrators of Zakat, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing captives, debtors, in the cause of Allah, and stranded travelers.

questions.q: What is meant by "Utility" in economic terms?
questions.m: Utility is the ability or power of a good or service to satisfy a specific human need. It represents the inherent capacity of an economic product to fulfill wants. For example, the utility of a book is its inherent power to satisfy the desire for knowledge, and the utility of a car is its inherent power to satisfy the desire to travel quickly from one place to another.

questions.q: Define "Commodity" and list its conditions in Islamic economics.
questions.m: A commodity is a tangible economic product that has a physical form. In Islamic economics, a commodity must meet four conditions: (1) It must be beneficial - providing utility to users, (2) It must be relatively rare - not infinitely available, (3) It must be tradable - able to be exchanged among society members, and (4) It must be permissible (Halal) according to Islamic law - this condition is unique to Islamic economics and takes precedence over the other conditions.

questions.q: What is "Jizya" and who was required to pay it?
questions.m: Jizya is a per capita yearly tax historically levied by Islamic states on certain non-Muslim subjects (dhimmi) living under Islamic law. It was paid in exchange for protection from outside aggression, exemption from military service, and the right to practice their faith with communal autonomy. Jizya was primarily required from free, sane, adult males among the dhimmi community (Jews, Christians, and others). Exempted from paying were women, children, the elderly, the poor, the handicapped, slaves, monks, and hermits.

questions.q: What is the correct definition of "Relative Scarcity" in Islamic economics?
o: The earth does not have enough resources to sustain the human population
The impossibility of providing every human with all their needs in the appropriate time, place, and form
The unequal distribution of wealth between rich and poor nations
The inability of governments to manage economic resources efficiently
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Relative scarcity means it is impossible to meet ALL human needs in the right time, place, and form - NOT that resources are globally insufficient.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what are the TWO roles of relative scarcity in Islam?
o: A warning sign and a reason for charity
A motive to work and a divine test requiring patience
An economic problem and a social issue
A punishment from Allah and a call for Zakah
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Relative scarcity serves two roles: (1) it motivates work and earth development, and (2) it is a divine test requiring patience.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a reason for starvation according to the Islamic perspective?
o: Unequal distribution of wealth and population
Absolute shortage of the earth's resources
Spiritual crisis making people indifferent to the poor
People's failure to use what Allah has given them
questions.e: ✓ Correct. "Absolute shortage of resources" is NOT a listed reason. Islam rejects this - resources are sufficient; the issue is distribution, behaviour, and spiritual failure.

questions.q: In Islam, what is the definition of "Capital" as a production element?
o: The total income earned by a person from their labour
The portion of wealth used to produce goods and services
Money saved in a bank for future use
Any natural resource found in the earth
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Capital is defined as the portion of wealth used in the production process (machines, tools, buildings).

questions.q: What is the key difference between "Musaqah" and "Muzara'ah"?
o: Musaqah involves cultivating bare land; Muzara'ah involves existing crops
Musaqah involves irrigating existing crops; Muzara'ah involves cultivating bare land
Both involve cultivating bare land, but the profit-sharing differs
Musaqah is for animals; Muzara'ah is for crops
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Musaqah = owner gives existing CROPS to be irrigated (think "S" for Sapling). Muzara'ah = owner gives bare LAND to be cultivated (think "Z" for Zero/starting from scratch).

questions.q: The Prophet ﷺ said "Indeed, Allah loves that when one of you does a job, he does it with excellence." This refers to which work ethic?
questions.e: ✓ Correct. This hadith refers specifically to "Mastery" (Itqan / إتقان) - doing one's work with excellence and precision.

questions.q: What distinguishes "Saving" from "Hoarding" in Islamic economics?
o: Saving is for the rich; hoarding is for the poor
Saving involves paying Zakah; hoarding withholds money from circulation without Zakah
There is no difference; both are prohibited in Islam
Saving is short-term; hoarding is long-term
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Saving = setting aside income for investment/emergencies while paying Zakah (good). Hoarding = withholding money from circulation WITHOUT paying Zakah (forbidden).

questions.q: In Islamic consumption theory, what does "Taraf" (ترف) refer to?
o: Spending money on wrongful and unworthy things
A luxury lifestyle characterized by indulgent extravagance
Exceeding the limit of temperance in spending
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Taraf = luxury lifestyle (most extreme level). Example: eating from gold utensils. It was the cause of punishment for past nations.

questions.q: The Quran says "spendthrifts are brothers of the devils." Which Arabic term does this describe?
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Tabthear (تبذير) = spending on wrongful/unworthy things. The Quran calls spendthrifts (Muthabthireen) "brothers of the devils."

questions.q: In the Islamic concept of gratification (إشباع), which of the following is TRUE compared to the non-Islamic concept?
o: Islam allows the consumer absolute authority to consume whatever they wish
Islam views gratification as both material and spiritual, requiring halal commodities
More consumption always leads to greater happiness in Islamic thought
Islam views interest as purely material enjoyment
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Islamic gratification includes both material AND spiritual dimensions, and the commodity must be halal. Unlike non-Islamic economics, more consumption does not automatically mean more happiness.

questions.q: What is the definition of "Market" in Islamic economic thought?
o: A government-controlled space where goods are distributed equally
An arrangement where sellers and buyers meet, exchange, and pricing is determined
A place where only halal goods are traded under strict supervision
A virtual concept with no physical boundaries
questions.e: ✓ Correct. A market is an arrangement where sellers and buyers meet, exchange, and pricing is determined. It is not exclusively government-controlled nor exclusively physical.

questions.q: When selling gold for silver (different types of usurious goods), Islamic law requires:
o: Immediate exchange only; different amounts are permitted
No special conditions - it is treated as a normal transaction
Equal amounts only; timing is flexible
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Different types (gold ↔ silver, riyal ↔ dollar): different amounts are ALLOWED, but immediate exchange is REQUIRED. Only same-type transactions require equal amounts.

questions.q: What is "Najash" (false bidding) and who bears responsibility for it?
o: A real buyer overbidding; only the buyer is responsible
A fake bidder raising prices without intent to buy; both seller and fake bidder sin
Price manipulation by the government; the state is responsible
Monopoly practices; only the monopolist is at fault
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Najash = a fake bidder raises the price without intending to buy, tricking a real buyer. Both the seller (who benefits) and the fake bidder share in the sin.

questions.q: The Prophet ﷺ said: "If anyone withholds grain for forty days seeking a high price, he has renounced God." This refers to which prohibition?
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Monopoly (Ihtikaar / احتكار) - withholding goods to drive up prices is one of the gravest market sins in Islam.

questions.q: When the Prophet ﷺ was asked to set prices during a price rise, he refused. What was his reason?
o: Governments have no right to interfere in any market matter
Allah is the one who sets prices, and he hoped to meet Allah without claims of injustice
The price rise was caused by human greed and should be investigated first
Trade agreements prevented him from interfering
questions.e: ✓ Correct. The Prophet ﷺ refused because he attributed natural price fluctuations to Allah's decree, and he did not want to commit an injustice in property matters.

questions.q: According to Islamic economics, in which situation does the ruler have the RIGHT to intervene and set prices?
o: When prices rise due to natural supply and demand
When prices rise due to monopoly, greed, or injustice by traders
The ruler can never interfere with prices in any situation
questions.e: ✓ Correct. The ruler intervenes ONLY when prices rise due to human injustice: monopoly, greed, or cheating - not natural supply/demand movements.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes "Mudarabah" (Brokerage)?
o: Two partners both contributing money in equal shares
One partner provides capital; the other provides effort; profits shared by agreement
A single person trading with their own money alone
The government providing funds to citizens for investment
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Mudarabah (Brokerage): one party provides the capital, the other provides the labour/effort, and profits are shared according to their agreement.

questions.q: Malthus claimed population growth outstrips resources. Which of these is a valid Islamic rebuttal?
o: Population must be limited by the government to match resources
Alternatives to exhausted resources emerge, and some resources (like fish) renew themselves
Malthus was correct and this is why poverty exists
Technology alone solves all resource shortages
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Islam refutes Malthus with 3 points: (1) some resources renew (fish, forests), (2) alternatives emerge when resources deplete, (3) studies disproved his global predictions.

questions.q: What does the Quran mean by "do not let your hand be tied to your neck, nor stretch it out fully"?
o: Be neither a miser nor a spendthrift - follow the middle path of moderation
Give all of your wealth in charity
Do not engage in manual labour
questions.e: ✓ Correct. This verse commands moderation: "tied hand to neck" = miserliness; "stretch it fully" = extravagance. Islam requires the middle path.

questions.q: What was the sin that caused Allah to destroy the people of Prophet Shu'ayb (peace be upon him)?
questions.e: ✓ Correct. Cheating in weights and measures was the sin of the people of Shu'ayb (AS). Allah destroyed them for this transgression.

questions.q: Relative Scarcity means the earth does not possess sufficient resources to provide a good life for humanity globally.
questions.e: ✗ FALSE. Relative Scarcity does NOT mean the earth lacks enough resources. Resources are sufficient globally for a good life. The issue is distribution, human behaviour, and inability to meet ALL desires simultaneously.

questions.q: In the Islamic concept, production becomes an act of worship (ibadah) when paired with sincere intention (niyyah).
questions.e: ✓ TRUE. Islam is unique in making production an act of worship (ibadah) when linked to sincere intention (niyyah). The Prophet ﷺ confirmed this: "The value of an action depends on the intention behind it."

questions.q: When selling gold for gold (same type of usurious goods), Islamic law only requires immediate exchange - the amounts do not need to be equal.
questions.e: ✗ FALSE. For same-type usurious goods (gold for gold), BOTH conditions are required: (1) equal amounts AND (2) immediate exchange. Only different-type exchanges allow unequal amounts.

questions.q: According to Islamic economics, the government is always allowed to set prices regardless of the reason for the price increase.
questions.e: ✗ FALSE. The government may ONLY intervene when prices rise due to monopoly or human injustice. When prices rise naturally (supply & demand), the Prophet ﷺ refused to intervene, saying Allah is the price-setter.

questions.q: In Islamic economics, "Israf" (إسراف) is considered more extreme than "Taraf" (ترف).
questions.e: ✗ FALSE. It is the OPPOSITE. Taraf (luxury lifestyle) is MORE extreme than Israf (exceeding limits in spending). Israf is less severe, while Taraf represents full indulgence in luxury.
